title: What the James Webb Space Telescope Changed About Our Understanding of the Early Universe
briefDescription: The first images from JWST rewrote what we thought we knew about galaxy formation — and posed questions we still can't answer.
targets: Amateur astronomers, science enthusiasts, anyone who watched the first JWST images drop and wanted to understand what they were seeing.
body:
The First Images

When NASA released the first deep-field image from JWST in July 2022, astronomers around the world stopped what they were doing. The image showed galaxies as they existed just 300 million years after the Big Bang — far older, larger, and more structured than the Standard Model of cosmology predicted they should be.

Why the Early Galaxies Were a Surprise

Existing models suggested that early galaxies should be small, irregular, and relatively dim — the universe hadn't had enough time to assemble large structures. JWST found galaxies that were massive, disk-shaped, and luminous at redshifts that put them within the first 600 million years of cosmic history. Something about how we model galaxy formation was incomplete.

The Hubble Tension Gets Worse

The Hubble constant — the rate at which the universe is expanding — has two main measurement methods that disagree with each other by about 8%. JWST's measurements of Cepheid variable stars tightened the error bars on one method without resolving the discrepancy. The tension is real. It may point to physics beyond the Standard Model.

What Comes Next

JWST is designed to last at least 20 years. It will characterise exoplanet atmospheres, probe the chemistry of molecular clouds, and continue pushing our models of the first billion years. Each answer it provides seems to generate three new questions — which is exactly what a good telescope should do.

title: Living on Mars: What We'd Actually Need to Solve
briefDescription: Setting aside the inspiration and the PR — here's the engineering and biology checklist before any human colony becomes viable.
targets: Space enthusiasts, readers of science fiction curious about plausibility, anyone following Mars missions.
body:
The Radiation Problem Is Underrated

Mars has no global magnetic field and an atmosphere one percent the density of Earth's. A human on the surface receives roughly 0.7 millisieverts per day — about 250 millisieverts per year. NASA's career limit for astronauts is 600 millisieverts. You'd burn through three years of career radiation budget in less than three years of Martian surface time. Underground habitats are not optional.

Dust That Gets Into Everything

Martian dust is fine, pervasive, and toxic. It contains perchlorates — oxidising compounds that are harmful to thyroid function and that colonise every surface they touch. The 2018 global dust storm lasted months and nearly killed the Opportunity rover. Any life-support system, solar panel array, or spacesuit seal has to account for a substance that will try to infiltrate everything.

The Psychological Dimension

The minimum Earth-Mars transit at current propulsion technology is about seven months each way. Communication delay ranges from 3 to 22 minutes. A medical emergency, a mental health crisis, or a conflict between crew members cannot be escalated to Earth in real time. The crew has to be autonomous in ways that no Antarctic expedition or submarine crew has been required to be.

In-Situ Resource Utilisation

Sending every kilogram to Mars costs approximately $10,000. The entire project hinges on making things on Mars from Martian materials — water ice from the poles, CO2 from the atmosphere for fuel, regolith for construction. NASA's MOXIE experiment on Perseverance demonstrated oxygen production from CO2. It was a small but genuinely important proof of concept.

title: The Fermi Paradox in 2025: Where Does the Debate Stand?
briefDescription: Decades after Fermi asked 'where is everybody?', we have much more data — and the silence is getting harder to explain.
targets: Anyone fascinated by the question of extraterrestrial life, science readers, SETI followers.
body:
The Original Question

In 1950, Enrico Fermi was having lunch at Los Alamos when he asked a deceptively simple question: given the age of the galaxy and the number of stars, if intelligent life is even moderately common, we should have seen evidence of it by now. The galaxy is 13 billion years old. A civilisation with even modestly better technology than ours should have been able to colonise it entirely in a fraction of that time. So where are they?

The Great Filter

Robin Hanson's 1998 essay proposed the Great Filter: somewhere on the path from simple chemistry to interstellar civilisation, there is a step that almost nothing survives. Either the filter is behind us — the emergence of complex life is extraordinarily rare — or it is ahead of us, which is the terrifying interpretation. Finding simple life on Mars would be the worst possible news.

What SETI Has Actually Found

Sixty-plus years of radio telescope surveys have found no unambiguous signal of extraterrestrial intelligence. The Wow! signal in 1977 was never repeated. Tabby's Star's unusual light curves, once speculated to be a megastructure, turned out to be consistent with dust clouds. The silence is genuine and well-documented.

The Zoo Hypothesis and Its Problems

Perhaps advanced civilisations are observing us but choosing not to make contact. This requires an implausibly perfect coordination across all civilisations across all of history — a single defector would break the embargo. The hypothesis is unfalsifiable in a way that should make us suspicious of it as an explanation.

title: How Black Holes Actually Work (Without the Hand-Waving)
briefDescription: A rigorous but accessible explanation of event horizons, Hawking radiation, and why black holes are stranger than most science writing admits.
targets: Curious non-physicists who want the real story, students, anyone who watched Interstellar and had questions.
body:
What a Black Hole Actually Is

A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is strong enough that nothing — including light — can escape. The boundary is called the event horizon. It's not a surface; it's a point of no return. An observer falling through the event horizon wouldn't feel anything special at that moment — they'd only know they'd crossed it when they couldn't get back.

The Singularity Problem

At the centre of a black hole, general relativity predicts a singularity — infinite density, infinite curvature. Physicists don't believe singularities are real. They're a signal that the theory has broken down and a more complete theory — quantum gravity — is needed. The singularity is a gap in our knowledge, not a description of nature.

Hawking Radiation

Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that black holes aren't completely black. Quantum effects near the event horizon cause the black hole to radiate energy slowly and lose mass. For stellar-mass black holes, the temperature is a fraction of a degree above absolute zero — completely undetectable. For microscopic black holes, it would be explosive. No microscopic black holes have been detected.

The Information Paradox

If a black hole evaporates completely via Hawking radiation, what happens to the information about everything that fell in? Quantum mechanics says information cannot be destroyed. General relativity says it is. The black hole information paradox is one of the deepest unsolved problems in theoretical physics and was the subject of a famous decades-long debate between Hawking and Susskind.

title: Amateur Astronomy: What You Can Actually See With a $400 Telescope
briefDescription: Honest expectations, the best targets for beginners, and why the most important piece of equipment is your dark-sky location.
targets: People considering getting into amateur astronomy, gift-buyers, anyone who looked up and wanted to see more.
body:
Managing Expectations

The images in astronomy magazines were taken with hours-long exposures by computerised mounts in dark-sky locations. With a $400 telescope in a suburban backyard, you will not see what you've seen in photos. What you will see is still remarkable: the craters on the moon in extraordinary detail, the bands of Jupiter and its four Galilean moons, the rings of Saturn, star clusters that look like scattered diamonds. This is not a consolation prize.

The Moon Is a Great First Target

The terminator — the line between the lit and dark halves — is where shadows are longest and surface detail most dramatic. A small telescope on a clear night reveals hundreds of named craters, mountain ranges, and ancient lava plains. It never gets old.

Light Pollution Is Your Biggest Enemy

A mediocre telescope under a dark sky outperforms an excellent telescope under city lights. The Bortle Dark-Sky Scale rates locations from 1 (truly dark) to 9 (inner-city). Under a Class 4 sky, the Milky Way is obvious to the naked eye. Under Class 8, only the moon and planets are worth looking at. Know your Bortle class before buying any equipment.

Start With a Refractor or a Dobsonian

Refractors (traditional lenses) are low-maintenance and great for planetary viewing. Dobsonians (large mirrors in simple mounts) give the most aperture per dollar for deep-sky objects. Both are more forgiving for beginners than computerised goto mounts, which are impressive until they need calibration at 11pm in the cold.

title: Prometheus and the Price of Knowledge: A Reading of the Myth
briefDescription: What the story of Prometheus stealing fire from the gods actually meant to ancient Greeks — and why it still resonates.
targets: Mythology enthusiasts, readers interested in ancient Greek thought, anyone curious about how myths encode cultural values.
body:
The Original Story

In Hesiod's Theogony, Prometheus steals fire from the gods and gives it to humanity. Zeus, enraged, has him chained to a rock in the Caucasus where an eagle eats his liver daily — it regenerates each night, so the torment is eternal. The story is not primarily about fire. It's about the consequences of transgressing divine order on behalf of humans who didn't ask for the gift and didn't fully understand its cost.

What Fire Represented

Fire in the Greek world was technology, civilisation, and the capacity for self-determination. Prometheus doesn't just give warmth — he gives humanity the means to cook, forge metal, light the dark, and eventually build cities. The myth encodes a genuine ambivalence about progress: the same fire that warms also burns. The same technology that elevates can destroy.

Aeschylus's Version

In Prometheus Bound, Aeschylus transforms the myth into a study of power and suffering. Prometheus is not a criminal but a martyr — he suffers because he knew what Zeus would do and did it anyway. He is also a prophet who cannot share his knowledge of Zeus's eventual downfall. The play asks what it means to know the future and be unable to change the present.

Prometheus in the Modern World

Shelley's Prometheus Unbound, Frankenstein (the subtitle is The Modern Prometheus), and a dozen Silicon Valley company logos all draw from the same well. The archetype of the innovator who transgresses boundaries and suffers for it remains one of the most enduring in Western culture. We are still debating whether the fire was worth it.

title: The Trojan War: History, Myth, and the Line Between Them
briefDescription: What archaeology actually tells us about Troy, what Homer invented, and why the distinction matters less than you'd think.
targets: History and mythology readers, students of the ancient world, anyone who's read the Iliad or seen Troy.
body:
Was There a Real Troy?

Yes — almost certainly. The site at Hisarlik in northwestern Turkey has been excavated since Heinrich Schliemann's controversial digs in the 1870s. Archaeologists have identified nine major layers of occupation. Troy VIIa, dating to around 1180 BCE, shows evidence of fire, violence, and hasty burial — consistent with a siege. The geography matches Homer's descriptions of the surrounding plain.

What Homer Added

Homer likely composed the Iliad around the 8th century BCE, writing about events that were already 400 years old and filtered through oral tradition. The divine interventions, the heroes' supernatural qualities, the dramatic speeches — these are the poetic elaboration of a tradition, not transcription of historical record. But the core geography, the military technology, and the social structures are consistent with the Late Bronze Age.

The Collapse That Created the Myth

The Trojan War, if it happened, took place during the Bronze Age Collapse — one of history's most dramatic civilisational failures. Within decades, the Mycenaean palaces fell, the Hittite empire dissolved, Egyptian power contracted, and dozens of cities were destroyed. The Iliad may preserve the memory of the last great campaigns of a world that was about to end.

Why the Myth Survived Everything

The Iliad isn't a war story. It's a story about the cost of pride, the waste of heroism, and the grief of men who know they're going to die. Achilles' choice — a short, glorious life over a long, obscure one — is a choice every person with ambition understands. Homer packaged something true about human nature in a story beautiful enough to survive 2,800 years.

title: Athena, Aphrodite, and the Problem of Competing Excellences
briefDescription: Why the Judgement of Paris was always going to end badly — and what it reveals about Greek views on wisdom, beauty, and power.
targets: Mythology readers, philosophy students, anyone interested in how myths encode moral frameworks.
body:
The Contest

Eris, goddess of discord, throws a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' into a wedding feast. Three goddesses claim it: Hera (queen, power), Athena (wisdom, war), Aphrodite (love, beauty). Paris of Troy is asked to judge. Each goddess offers a bribe. He chooses Aphrodite's gift: Helen, the most beautiful mortal woman. The Trojan War follows.

Why This Is a Philosophical Thought Experiment

The Greeks were deeply interested in the question of what the best human life looks like. The three goddesses represent three genuine answers: political power and status (Hera), excellence in craft and strategy (Athena), erotic love and beauty (Aphrodite). Paris must choose between them. The myth suggests that this choice cannot be made without consequence — choosing one excellence means sacrificing the others.

Athena's Complexity

Athena is one of the most interesting figures in the Greek pantheon because she embodies contradictions. She is the goddess of both wisdom and war — a combination that would seem oxymoronic but that the Greeks considered natural. Strategic intelligence is what separates effective warfare from slaughter. She is also a virgin goddess in a mythology obsessed with erotic conquest, which says something about how the Greeks categorised intellectual excellence as outside the domain of eros.

What Paris's Choice Says

Paris doesn't choose foolishly by Greek standards. Love is a genuine good. But the myth frames his choice as the beginning of catastrophe, which encodes a warning: choosing one form of excellence in a way that ignores consequences for others leads to disaster. The apple was never meant to be caught by a mortal hand.

title: Orpheus and the Nature of Loss
briefDescription: The myth of Orpheus and Eurydice is about grief — and why looking back is sometimes the most human thing you can do.
targets: Readers interested in mythology and its emotional depth, people who've experienced loss, lovers of Hadestown.
body:
The Story

Orpheus is the greatest musician in the Greek world — his music can move rivers and calm wild animals. When his wife Eurydice dies from a snakebite, he descends into the Underworld and uses his music to persuade Hades and Persephone to allow her to return. The condition: he must walk ahead of her on the way back and not look back until they've both crossed into the living world. He looks back. She returns to the dead.

Why He Looked

The myth doesn't explain this clearly, and that ambiguity is its power. Classical interpretations include: he doubted the gods' promise; he couldn't bear the uncertainty of whether she was really there; love cannot exist without verification, without confirmation of presence. The philosopher's reading is that Orpheus demonstrates the impossibility of trusting the divine promise of restoration. The poet's reading is simpler — he looked because he loved her.

The Music After

What happens to Orpheus after he loses Eurydice the second time is in some ways more interesting than the descent. He wanders, plays music of pure grief, and eventually is torn apart by Maenads — in some versions because he refuses to honour Dionysus, in others because the women are furious he's sworn off romantic love. His head, still singing, floats down a river to Lesbos, where it becomes an oracle.

Why This Myth Endures

Every major artistic period has produced a version of Orpheus — Monteverdi's opera, Gluck's opera, Jean Cocteau's films, Hadestown. The myth endures because it says something true: the hardest part of grief is not the descent into it, but the attempt to leave it behind without looking back.

title: Medea: The Most Disturbing Play in Greek Drama
briefDescription: Euripides' Medea broke every rule of Greek tragedy — and its portrait of a woman pushed beyond limit is still almost unbearable to read.
targets: Classical literature readers, drama enthusiasts, feminists interested in how ancient texts handle female agency.
body:
The Context

Medea premiered in Athens in 431 BCE. It was third place in its year's competition — which tells you everything about how uncomfortable Athenian audiences found it. Euripides was always the difficult one, the tragedian who gave his characters psychology instead of just function. Medea is his most unsettling creation.

Who Medea Is

Medea is a foreign woman — from Colchis, near the Black Sea — who betrayed her father, killed her brother, and fled her homeland to help Jason get the Golden Fleece. She is a sorceress, an exile, and a mother. When Jason abandons her to marry a Greek princess, she has no legal recourse, no home to return to, and no identity outside her connection to him. What she does have is knowledge of poisons.

The Murder of the Children

Most shocking is that Medea kills her own children — not in a blind rage but after a long, agonised deliberation that Euripides puts on stage in real time. She goes back and forth, argues with herself, and then does it. The play forces the audience to understand, not just witness. That's what made it so disturbing then and now.

The Feminist Reading and Its Limits

Medea is often read as a proto-feminist text — a woman punishing a man who treated her as property. This reading is true but incomplete. Euripides is less interested in making Medea a hero than in showing what happens to a person when every structural support for their identity is destroyed. The children are casualties of Jason's betrayal as much as Medea's revenge.

title: Why King Lear Is Shakespeare's Most Devastating Play
briefDescription: A close reading of why Lear's tragedy cuts deeper than Hamlet or Macbeth — and what makes the ending almost impossible to stage.
targets: Shakespeare readers, theatregoers, students of English literature, anyone who wants to understand what the fuss is about.
body:
The Premise

Lear, an old king, divides his kingdom between his daughters based on how much they profess to love him. His two elder daughters flatter him. His youngest, Cordelia, refuses to perform love in these terms and says nothing beyond the truth. He disinherits her. Within two acts, he has lost everything — his authority, his home, his sanity, and finally his mind — while his honest daughter fights a war to rescue him.

What Makes Lear Different from Other Tragedies

Hamlet dies because of circumstances and delay. Macbeth dies because of ambition and guilt. Lear's tragedy is more fundamental: he is destroyed by the gap between what love should be and what the world is actually like. He expected the universe to reward fidelity and virtue. The play demonstrates, with pitiless thoroughness, that it does not.

The Fool

The Fool is one of Shakespeare's strangest creations — he speaks truth to power through riddles and jokes, the only character who can tell Lear directly that he's made a catastrophic mistake. He disappears from the play halfway through without explanation, having served his function. Some scholars believe the same actor played both the Fool and Cordelia in the original productions, which would make the doubling a theatrical statement about wisdom and love as two faces of the same thing.

The Ending

Cordelia is hanged off-stage and dies in Lear's arms. Lear dies of grief. Nahum Tate rewrote the play in 1681 with a happy ending — Cordelia and Edgar marry, Lear is restored to power — and that version was performed for 150 years because audiences couldn't bear the original. Dr. Johnson said he couldn't reread the last act. The original ending is not nihilism; it's something harder — the refusal to console.

title: Reading Hamlet as a Play About Delay
briefDescription: Why Hamlet doesn't act is the wrong question. The right question is what Shakespeare is saying about the relationship between thought and action.
targets: Shakespeare enthusiasts, philosophy readers, anyone who has studied or seen Hamlet and wanted to go deeper.
body:
The Famous Problem

Hamlet is asked by his father's ghost to avenge his murder. He takes five acts to do it. Coleridge said Hamlet had too much reflection and too little action. Goethe said the task was simply too large for him. Freud, inevitably, said it was Oedipal. None of these explanations is fully satisfying, which is why scholars are still arguing about it four centuries later.

The Play-Within-the-Play

Hamlet's most revealing line is 'The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.' Rather than acting on the ghost's evidence, he stages a theatrical reenactment to verify it. This is a man who needs more evidence than a supernatural testimony. He wants empirical confirmation. The delay isn't cowardice — it's epistemology.

What Hamlet Is Afraid Of

He says it directly in the 'To be or not to be' soliloquy: the fear is not death but 'what dreams may come' in the undiscovered country. He's worried about damnation — both his own if he kills without certainty, and his father's if the ghost is a devil luring him to sin. The play is saturated with theological anxiety about what lies beyond.

The First Quarto's Hamlet

The 1603 'bad quarto' of Hamlet is shorter, rougher, and probably records an early touring version of the play. It has a famous alternative version of the 'To be or not to be' speech. Reading it alongside the familiar text shows how the play was revised and refined — and how much of what we think of as Hamlet is a specific editorial construction, not the one true text.

title: How the Metaphysical Poets Reinvented English Verse
briefDescription: Donne, Herbert, Marvell — and why their strange, knotty, intellectual poetry was the most alive thing happening in 17th-century England.
targets: Poetry readers, students of English literature, anyone who's encountered metaphysical poetry and wanted context.
body:
What 'Metaphysical' Means

Dr. Johnson coined the term disparagingly in 1779 — he thought the metaphysical poets were showing off their learning at the expense of genuine feeling. He was half right. Donne, Herbert, Marvell, Crashaw, and Vaughan all wrote poems dense with philosophical argument, scientific metaphor, and logical paradox. But the argument and the feeling are the same thing in their best work, not opposites.

John Donne's Conceits

A conceit is an extended, elaborate metaphor that the poem develops through sustained logic. Donne's most famous is in 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning' — he compares two lovers' souls to the two legs of a geometric compass. The 'fixed foot' (the absent beloved) makes the other circle back to its starting point. This is either ridiculous or profound. The poem insists it's both.

George Herbert's Architecture

Herbert was a priest, and his collection The Temple is structured like a church — poems arranged to reflect a spiritual journey. But his individual poems are formally extraordinary. 'Easter Wings' is shaped like two wings on the page. 'The Altar' is shaped like an altar. These aren't tricks — the form enacts the argument, so the poem means something different to read than to hear.

Why They Matter Now

T.S. Eliot revived interest in the metaphysicals in the 1920s because they did something he thought modern poetry had lost: unified thought and feeling without sentimentality. The idea that a poem could be intellectually rigorous and emotionally devastating at the same time was radical in 1920 and is still instructive now.

title: The Brontë Sisters: Three Writers, One Remarkable Year
briefDescription: In 1847, three sisters published three extraordinary novels. The story of how Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell became Charlotte, Emily, and Anne.
targets: Literary history readers, Brontë fans, anyone interested in women's writing and Victorian publishing.
body:
The Pen Names

The Brontë sisters — Charlotte, Emily, and Anne — published their 1847 novels under the male pseudonyms Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. This wasn't unusual for women writers of the period; George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans) took the same approach. The motivation was partly commercial — male authors sold better — and partly a desire to be judged on merit rather than dismissed as female amateurs.

Three Completely Different Books

Jane Eyre (Charlotte) is a domestic romance with a gothic undercurrent. Wuthering Heights (Emily) is a strange, violent, formally unusual novel that contemporary reviewers found alarming. The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (Anne) is the most directly feminist of the three — it depicts a woman leaving an abusive alcoholic husband and was considered so controversial that Charlotte suppressed its republication after Anne died.

The Parsonage in Haworth

The sisters grew up in the parsonage at Haworth, Yorkshire, a bleak moorland town with one of the highest child mortality rates in England. Their father, an Irish-born clergyman, was unusual in giving his daughters a serious education. Their childhood fantasies — the imaginary kingdoms of Angria and Gondal — were elaborate enough to fill thousands of handwritten pages and were probably the rehearsal space for their adult fiction.

Emily's Brief Life

Emily Brontë published one novel, Wuthering Heights, and died of tuberculosis the year after at 30. She refused medical treatment and was said to have been working until two days before she died. Wuthering Heights was poorly received in 1847 and is now considered one of the strangest and most original novels in the English language. The gap between initial reception and eventual reputation is a useful corrective to contemporary criticism.

title: On Rereading Books: Why the Second Reading Is Always Different
briefDescription: What changes when you return to a book you first read at 17 — and what that tells you about how we read and how we change.
targets: Readers, anyone who has returned to a loved book and been surprised, people interested in the psychology of reading.
body:
The Book That Changed

I first read Middlemarch at 22 and found it admirable but dense. I reread it at 37 and could barely put it down. The novel hadn't changed. The experience of reading it was almost unrecognisable. The difference was that I had now made some of the choices Dorothea is making — about work, commitment, the sacrifice of one vision of life for another. The book had become about me in a way it couldn't have been at 22.

What Rereading Reveals About First Readings

First readings are about plot — what happens next. Rereading is about everything else: structure, foreshadowing, thematic repetition, the gap between what characters say and what they mean. Nabokov famously said that we do not read books, we reread them, and he wasn't being pretentious — a first reading genuinely doesn't give you enough to see the whole thing.

Books That Reward Rereading

Not all books reward rereading equally. Plot-driven genre fiction usually doesn't — once you know who did it, the experience is fundamentally changed. Literary fiction that operates through language and structure rather than plot often gets better. Poetry almost always does. The test is whether there's more than mechanics holding the thing together.

The Rereading List

I keep a short list of books I return to every five years or so: Middlemarch, Anna Karenina, a handful of Chekhov stories, The Great Gatsby. Each reading is also a measurement — of what I've learned, what I've lost, what has changed in my own understanding. The books are landmarks. The distance between readings is the journey.

title: The Battle of Vimy Ridge and What It Meant for Canada
briefDescription: April 9, 1917 — four divisions fought together for the first time as a single Canadian force. Why this battle became a founding myth.
targets: Canadian history readers, WWI enthusiasts, anyone interested in how nations construct national identity through military history.
body:
The Strategic Context

Vimy Ridge was a heavily fortified German position in northern France that British and French forces had failed to take at enormous cost. The Canadian Corps — four divisions fighting together for the first time under Canadian command — was assigned the assault in April 1917. The planning was meticulous: every soldier had studied a plaster model of the terrain, rehearsed their specific role, and knew what to do if their officer fell.

The Battle

Easter Monday, April 9, 1917, at 5:30 in the morning, 30,000 Canadian soldiers advanced behind a rolling artillery barrage in a snowstorm. In four days, they took a position that had resisted all previous attempts. The cost was 3,598 Canadian dead and more than 7,000 wounded. The method — careful preparation, decentralised command, combined arms coordination — would influence Allied tactics for the rest of the war.

The Myth That Followed

The historian Pierre Berton called Vimy Ridge the birth of Canadian nationhood — the moment the country came into its own sense of itself as distinct from Britain. This is partly true and partly constructed. Canada had been asserting itself diplomatically for decades. But Vimy gave a specific, dramatic, successful moment around which national feeling could crystallise, which is what myths do even when they simplify.

The Monument

The Walter Allward memorial at Vimy Ridge, unveiled in 1936, is one of the most moving war monuments in the world. The two white pylons represent Canada and France. The cloaked figures represent mourning, hope, and justice. At the base, the names of 11,285 Canadian soldiers who died in France with no known grave. Allward spent 11 years designing it.

title: Reconstruction and Its Unfinished Business
briefDescription: The decade after the Civil War when Black Americans held political office, built institutions — and why it was violently ended.
targets: American history readers, people interested in the roots of contemporary racial inequality, anyone who wants to understand what was possible and what was destroyed.
body:
What Reconstruction Was

Reconstruction (1865–1877) was the federal attempt to rebuild the South after the Civil War while integrating formerly enslaved people as full citizens. The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments abolished slavery, established birthright citizenship, and guaranteed voting rights. For a brief period, it worked: Black men voted, ran for office, and served as senators and governors. More than 2,000 Black Americans held elected office during Reconstruction.

What It Built

Reconstruction governments built the South's first public school systems, reformed tax structures to reduce aristocratic privilege, invested in infrastructure, and established hospitals and institutions for formerly enslaved people. These achievements were real and significant. They were also deeply threatening to the old planter class, which organised to destroy them.

The Overthrow

Reconstruction ended not through democratic process but through organised violence. The Ku Klux Klan and other terrorist groups systematically murdered Black political leaders, burned churches and schools, and intimidated voters. The federal government, under President Grant, initially fought back. Eventually, Northern political will eroded. The Compromise of 1877 ended federal enforcement in the South. What followed was Jim Crow.

The Lost History

For most of the 20th century, Reconstruction was taught as a mistake — a period of corrupt government imposed on the South by carpetbaggers and incompetent Black officials. This was the Dunning School interpretation, and it was systematically false. The revisionist history, led by W.E.B. Du Bois in Black Reconstruction (1935) and confirmed by subsequent scholarship, has overturned it. But the Dunning version shaped American self-understanding for generations.

title: The Fur Trade and the Making of Canada
briefDescription: How the competition for beaver pelts shaped North American geography, Indigenous diplomacy, and eventually the borders of a country.
targets: Canadian history buffs, students of colonial history, readers interested in how economic forces shape nations.
body:
Why Beaver?

European hatmakers in the 17th century had exhausted their supply of beaver fur, which was essential for producing the felt used in fashionable hats. North America had an almost unlimited supply and a network of Indigenous peoples who were skilled trappers and eager traders. Within decades of contact, the fur trade had become the dominant economic and political force in the northern half of the continent.

The Hudson's Bay Company

Chartered in 1670, the Hudson's Bay Company was granted exclusive trading rights over all lands draining into Hudson Bay — a territory called Rupert's Land, encompassing much of what is now central Canada. The Company built forts, established diplomatic relationships with dozens of Indigenous nations, and essentially governed the interior of the continent for two centuries. Canada acquired Rupert's Land in 1870 for £300,000.

Indigenous Agency in the Trade

For most of the fur trade's history, Indigenous peoples were not passive victims but active agents who negotiated terms, played European powers against each other, and shaped the trade to their advantage. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy's strategic position between French and British spheres of influence gave them substantial leverage. The Cree and Ojibwe nations were central to the HBC supply chain and knew it.

The Long Decline

European fashion changed. By the 1840s, silk hats had replaced beaver felt, and the economic basis of the trade collapsed. What remained were the patterns of settlement, the trading relationships, the half-completed geography of a country whose borders had been drawn by rivers and forts rather than by any deliberate plan.

title: The Underground Railroad: What It Actually Was
briefDescription: Separating the mythology from the history — who ran it, how it worked, and what it cost.
targets: American history readers, anyone who wants to understand the real scale and mechanics of this extraordinary human effort.
body:
The Name and the Reality

The Underground Railroad was never a single organisation, never had a formal structure, and was not primarily underground. It was a loose network of people — Black and white, free and formerly enslaved — who provided food, shelter, transportation, and guidance to people escaping from slavery. It operated through trust and secrecy, not hierarchy.

The Numbers

Historians estimate that between 1850 and 1860 alone, somewhere between 1,000 and 5,000 people escaped via the Railroad each year. The total number who escaped slavery through various means over the antebellum period may have been 100,000 or more. These numbers are significant — but they also meant that the vast majority of the four million enslaved people in the South in 1860 had no realistic means of escape.

Harriet Tubman

Tubman escaped slavery in 1849 and returned to the South 13 times to guide others to freedom. She never lost a passenger. During the Civil War she served as a spy and scout for the Union Army, leading a raid that freed 700 enslaved people in a single night. Frederick Douglass wrote to her: 'I know of no one who has willingly encountered more perils and hardships to serve our enslaved people than you have.'

The Cost

The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required Northern states to return escaped enslaved people to their enslavers. It put free Black communities in the North at constant risk and made the Underground Railroad participants — including white helpers — federal criminals. The people who ran it knew exactly what they were risking.

title: How the Manhattan Project Changed the Relationship Between Science and the State
briefDescription: The bomb wasn't just a weapon — it created a new model for how governments fund and control scientific research.
targets: History of science readers, anyone interested in the political legacy of WWII, people curious about how Big Science began.
body:
Before the Project

Before 1940, most scientific research in the United States was funded by universities and private foundations. The federal government had almost no role in directing basic research. The Manhattan Project changed this permanently. At its peak, it employed 130,000 people, operated in dozens of secret facilities across North America, and cost approximately $2 billion — the equivalent of $30 billion today.

The Scientific Concentration

Los Alamos, the design laboratory in the New Mexico mountains, brought together the most remarkable concentration of scientific talent in history. Oppenheimer, Fermi, Bohr, Feynman, Bethe, Teller — the physicists who would define the second half of the 20th century were all there, under military secrecy, working on a problem with a deadline. The intellectual atmosphere was extraordinary and the moral weight was crushing.

The Aftermath

After the war, the model of government-funded large-scale research became the default for fields from particle physics to cancer research. The National Science Foundation, founded in 1950, institutionalised federal science funding. The Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) funded the research that eventually produced the internet. The state became the patron of science in ways that shaped what questions got asked and what didn't.

Oppenheimer's Regret

Robert Oppenheimer famously said that the physicists who built the bomb had 'known sin'. He spent the rest of his career arguing for international control of nuclear weapons and was eventually stripped of his security clearance in 1954 during the McCarthy era. The man who built the most destructive weapon in history became an advocate for the limitation of its use — and was punished for it by the government that built the weapon.

title: How I Fell in Love with Hockey Statistics
briefDescription: What advanced metrics actually tell you that traditional stats miss — and why Corsi is both revolutionary and misunderstood.
targets: Hockey fans curious about analytics, stats enthusiasts, anyone who's heard 'possession hockey' and wanted to know what it means.
body:
The Problem with Plus/Minus

Plus/minus — the number of goals scored for and against while a player is on the ice — is the traditional measure of defensive and two-way contribution. The problem is that it's almost entirely a measure of teammates and deployment. A good player on a bad team will have a terrible plus/minus. A mediocre player whose linemates happen to be great will have a great one. It measures context more than it measures player.

What Corsi Measures

Corsi (named after an analytics pioneer, Jim Corsi) counts all shot attempts — goals, shots on net, shots that miss, and shots that hit the post — and calculates the ratio for and against while a player is on the ice. Shots correlate much more strongly with winning than goals do over small sample sizes because they're more frequent and less affected by goaltending variance. Corsi is a proxy for puck possession.

The Limitations

Corsi doesn't capture zone starts (a player deployed in the offensive zone will have better Corsi than one deployed defensively), quality of competition, or individual defensive skill. Advanced analytics have evolved considerably since the basic Corsi era — RAPM metrics, expected goals models, and tracking data from cameras have produced increasingly sophisticated estimates of player value.

Why the Old Guard Resisted

The analytics movement in hockey faced enormous pushback from coaches and front offices who had built their careers on traditional scouting. Some of this was defensiveness; some was legitimate — there are real aspects of the game that numbers struggle to capture. The honest answer is that the best teams now use both. The war between eye test and spreadsheet was always a false choice.

title: The Greatest Games I've Ever Watched: A Hockey Fan's Personal List
briefDescription: Seven games — one from each decade since the 1970s — that show what hockey can be when everything comes together.
targets: Hockey fans, sports history readers, people who want to understand why hockey fans are the way they are.
body:
1980: Miracle on Ice

The US Olympic team — college students average age 21 — defeated the Soviet Union 4-3 in the medal round at Lake Placid. The Soviets hadn't lost an Olympic game since 1968. This wasn't an upset — it was an impossibility that happened anyway. Al Michaels' 'Do you believe in miracles? YES!' is the most famous sports call in American broadcasting history. I wasn't alive for it and still get chills.

1994: Game 7, Rangers vs. Canucks

The New York Rangers ended a 54-year Stanley Cup drought in Madison Square Garden. Mark Messier had guaranteed a win in Game 6 and delivered a hat trick. The series had everything — Bure's blazing speed, Richter's heroics, the Garden's electricity. When Messier lifted the Cup, you could feel the city exhale 54 years of waiting.

2010: Gold Medal Game, Canada vs. USA

Sidney Crosby. Overtime. Vancouver. Canada wins 3-2 with the longest 7.4 seconds in the history of a country. Ryan Miller was spectacular. Crosby's backhand was perfect. Every Canadian I know remembers where they were. I watched it in a bar and didn't speak for five minutes afterward.

2022: Game 6, Avalanche vs. Lightning

Colorado's Cup win felt inevitable by midseason and was still miraculous to watch. Cale Makar, 23, was the best player on the ice in every game of the finals. The Lightning had won two straight Cups and were the most complete team of their era. Watching a new dynasty begin is always bittersweet and always worth staying up for.

title: What It's Like to Coach Bantam Hockey
briefDescription: Three seasons coaching 14-year-olds through the most formative level of minor hockey — what I learned about the game and about people.
targets: Minor hockey parents, coaches at any level, anyone interested in the human side of youth sports.
body:
Why Bantam Is Different

Bantam (14-year-olds) is where hockey starts to separate. The kids who might have a future in the sport can start to see it. The kids who won't have one are starting to feel it. Everybody is going through puberty, which means the same player who was your most coachable in October is a completely different emotional system by February. The coaching is less about hockey and more about helping people figure out who they are.

What I Got Wrong in Year One

I ran practices the way my own coaches had run them — drills, more drills, systems. The kids were bored and I couldn't understand why the on-ice execution didn't match the practice. What I hadn't figured out was that engagement in practice is the variable. A drill done at 60% intensity because the kid is mentally elsewhere teaches worse habits than no drill at all. Year two I made every drill competitive and saw immediate improvement.

The Parent Problem

About 20% of minor hockey parents are the reason 20% of minor hockey kids quit by 16. The parents who've decided their child is a future NHL player, and communicate this to the child and the coach through every interaction, are putting an unbearable weight on a 14-year-old. The coaches who survive long-term in minor hockey have developed a specific, patient, firm way of having this conversation.

Why I Keep Coming Back

At the end of year three, one of my kids — who'd barely made the team and spent most of the year on the fourth line — scored the tying goal in the last minute of our last playoff game. We lost in overtime. He cried in the dressing room. Six months later he told me it was the best thing that had ever happened to him. That's the whole job right there.

title: The PWHL's First Season: What It Changed for Women's Hockey
briefDescription: The Professional Women's Hockey League launched in 2024 and drew 20,000 fans to a single regular-season game. What happened and why it matters.
targets: Women's hockey fans, sports business readers, anyone who's been following the long struggle for a viable professional women's league.
body:
The League Before the League

Women's professional hockey in North America had a history of failed leagues. The NWHL (later PHF) struggled with low salaries, inconsistent ownership, and minimal media coverage. The CWHL had better Canadian support but folded in 2019 citing financial unsustainability. The best women's hockey players in the world were playing for $15,000 a year or less — many had full-time jobs alongside their hockey.

The Big Four Involvement

The PWHL was launched with the backing of the NHL — specifically with ownership stakes held by the six original team owners. The salary structure was significantly better than anything that had preceded it. The league started with six teams in established hockey markets: Boston, Minnesota, Montreal, New York, Ottawa, and Toronto. The infrastructure — arenas, broadcast deals, medical staff, travel budgets — was professional from day one.

The Attendance Story

The Toronto Sceptres played a regular-season game at Scotiabank Arena — the same building where the Leafs play — and drew 19,285 fans. Montreal followed with a similar number. The narrative that women's hockey didn't have an audience was revealed to be not a statement about demand but about investment. When the product was properly resourced and marketed, people came.

What Still Needs to Happen

The PWHL has 24 players per roster and a salary cap well below what top NHL players make per week. The league is profitable in the way that a first-year startup is profitable — not yet, but with a plausible path. The expansion conversations are real. Whether the league builds on this foundation or becomes another cautionary tale depends on decisions being made right now about revenue sharing, broadcast rights, and whether the NHL sees this as a feeder system or a genuine co-investment.

title: Understanding Hockey's Neutral Zone: The Game Within the Game
briefDescription: The area between the blue lines decides more games than anyone who doesn't obsessively watch hockey realises.
targets: Hockey fans wanting to deepen their tactical understanding, players at the junior level, coaches looking for frameworks.
body:
Why the Neutral Zone Gets Ignored

Goals happen in the offensive zone. Saves happen in the defensive zone. The neutral zone is where neither of these exciting things occur — it's the highway between the interesting places. And yet: the team that controls neutral zone transitions wins far more games than the shot-attempt numbers alone explain. The gap between a possession-play team and a defensive-shell team is often negotiated entirely between the blue lines.

The Left-Wing Lock and Its Legacy

Scotty Bowman's Detroit Red Wings of the 1990s popularised the left-wing lock — a system where the left wing held back during offensive zone exits to form a 1-2-2 neutral zone trap rather than a traditional 2-1-2 forecheck. It was brutally effective and brutally boring. The NHL eventually changed rules on obstruction and icing specifically to allow teams to break out faster. The systems evolved in response.

The Modern Transition

Contemporary neutral zone play at the NHL level is about controlled exits (maintaining possession through the defensive zone end and out) and controlled entries (carrying or passing the puck across the offensive blue line in possession rather than dumping it in). Entry with possession leads to scoring chances at roughly twice the rate of dump-and-chase entries. This is not controversial among analysts; it's still controversial among coaches who built careers on forechecking.

What to Watch For

Next time you watch an NHL game, watch the D-zone exit. Does the defending team exit with a stretch pass to a forward across the neutral zone? Does the puck carrier gain the line with speed? Or does pressure force a dump to the centre ice? Those 3 seconds between the zones contain more of the game's decision-making than the 30 seconds of offensive zone time that follows.

title: Why I Stopped Chasing Frameworks and Started Reading Source Code
briefDescription: The habit that had the biggest impact on my growth as an engineer — and why most tutorials actively work against it.
targets: Developers at any level who feel stuck, anyone who learns from documentation but wants to go deeper.
body:
The Tutorial Trap

Tutorials teach you how to use a tool. Source code teaches you how the tool works. The gap between these two kinds of knowledge determines how you behave when the tutorial's assumptions break down — which is whenever the real world intrudes on the happy path. Most working software is not on the happy path.

Where to Start

Pick a library you use every day. Find the main entry point. Trace one operation from the public API through to the actual implementation. Don't try to understand everything — understand the path of one call. Express's request handling. React's reconciler for a simple re-render. Postgres.js's query execution. One path, completely, before expanding outward.

What You'll Find

The things you'll find are: design decisions you've been fighting against because you didn't understand the constraint they were solving; performance characteristics that explain why the thing you're doing is slow; error messages that will now make sense for the rest of your career because you saw where they're generated.

The Compound Effect

Every hour reading source code pays dividends for years. The mental model you build of how HTTP servers handle connections, how ORMs translate queries, how React batches state updates — these don't become obsolete when the framework version changes. The underlying ideas are stable. A developer who understands the ideas can learn any new framework in a weekend. One who only knows the API syntax starts over from scratch every three years.

title: The Humbling Experience of Maintaining an Open Source Library
briefDescription: What happens when strangers depend on your code — edge cases you never imagined, bug reports from environments you've never heard of.
targets: Developers thinking about open sourcing their work, contributors to open source, anyone curious about the realities of OSS maintenance.
body:
The First Real Issue

Six weeks after I published my first library — a small utility for parsing a specific file format — I got an issue from someone running it on a 900MB file. My tests had used files up to 2MB. The parser loaded the entire file into memory before processing it. The issue was correct, the fix was real work, and I had been living in a comfortable fiction about the edge cases I'd considered.

The Support Burden

Open source has a support channel that never closes and is always staffed by one person who has a day job. Issues come in at 2am from users in timezones you don't normally think about. Some issues are excellent, specific, and reproducible. Some are 'it doesn't work' with no further information. Learning to triage kindly — asking for more information without making the user feel bad for not providing it — is a skill that took me a year.

Semver Is a Social Contract

Semantic versioning — major.minor.patch — is a promise to users about what kind of changes to expect. The moment you break that promise by shipping breaking changes in a minor version, you damage trust. I did this once, with a change that seemed obviously non-breaking to me and was breaking for a significant subset of users. The lesson: what's 'obviously non-breaking' depends on use cases you haven't imagined yet.

What It Gave Me

Reading bug reports from environments, languages, and use cases I'd never imagined stretched my mental model of the problem space in ways no internal project ever had. The library forced me to think about guarantees, contracts, and compatibility as first-class design concerns. It also gave me three connections that led directly to job offers. The side-effect economy of OSS is underrated.

title: Debugging: The Skill Nobody Teaches Systematically
briefDescription: Why debugging is the highest-leverage skill in engineering and the specific mental habits that separate fast debuggers from slow ones.
targets: Developers at any level who want to get faster at finding and fixing bugs, engineering students, team leads building debugging culture.
body:
The Debugging Mindset

Most inexperienced debuggers approach bugs with hope: they make a change, run the code, and hope the problem went away. This is a random walk through the problem space. Experienced debuggers approach bugs with hypotheses: they form a theory about the cause, design a test that would falsify that theory, run it, and update the theory based on the result. The difference in speed is not marginal.

The Minimal Reproduction

The most useful thing you can do before debugging anything non-trivial is reduce it to the smallest possible program that exhibits the problem. Strip away everything that isn't necessary for the bug to occur. This process almost always reveals the cause before you've finished it — the constraint of removing things forces you to understand which things are relevant. If it doesn't reveal the cause, you now have something you can share with someone else without sharing your entire codebase.

Binary Search Through Time

If you have a codebase with version control and a bug that didn't exist in a previous version, git bisect will find the commit that introduced it faster than any other technique. You mark a known-good commit, a known-bad commit, and let git divide the history. Each test halves the search space. For a 1,000-commit history, you'll find it in about 10 tests.

Print Debugging Is Not Embarrassing

There is a persistent culture in engineering that print debugging (adding console.log / print / fmt.Println statements to trace execution) is primitive. It isn't. The right tool depends on the problem. Debuggers with breakpoints are excellent for synchronous problems in single-threaded code. Print debugging is often faster for concurrent systems, distributed systems, or problems that only appear in production environments where a debugger can't attach.

title: What the First Year of Engineering Management Taught Me
briefDescription: The skills that transferred from IC work, the ones that didn't, and the moments that revealed what leading a team actually requires.
targets: Senior engineers considering management, new engineering managers, people building mental models of the EM role.
body:
The Knowledge That Transferred

Technical context. The ability to understand what engineers are working on, why a problem is hard, where the complexity actually lives. Without this, a manager can't make good decisions about roadmap, hiring, or when to escalate. The engineers can smell when their manager doesn't understand the work, and it damages trust. Technical depth has a half-life in management but doesn't evaporate quickly.

The Knowledge That Didn't

Individual productivity. As an IC, I got satisfaction from shipping things. As a manager, I ship almost nothing directly. My job is to enable others to ship. For about four months this felt like a grievous loss and I kept sneaking off to write code instead of having the difficult conversation I was avoiding. The difficult conversation always mattered more.

What Nobody Told Me About 1-on-1s

The 1-on-1 is not a status update. Asking 'what did you work on this week?' is a waste of both of your time. The 1-on-1 is for things that won't come up in other forums: career concerns, interpersonal friction, blockers the engineer doesn't want to raise in the team, early signals of disengagement. It requires asking different questions and sitting with silence while the answer forms.

The Performance Conversation

The first time I had to tell someone their work wasn't meeting expectations, I had rehearsed for two days. I was still bad at it. The only way to get good at difficult feedback is to give it, debrief, and give it again. The managers I most admire deliver hard truths with specificity, care, and no drama. They've had the conversation a hundred times. There is no shortcut.
